effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative ethnographic study; no quantitative point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are estimated.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Constitutional recognition of the human right to water and formal piped connections to Nairobi Water do not secure reliable water access in practice; actualizing ('concretizing') water rights requires mobilizing interpersonal connections, sustained committee/political pressure, and informal payments with infrastructurally powerful utility actors (managers, distribution valve operators, and field plumbers). Well-connected middle-class Langata estate committees secure intermittent water flows and utility water trucks through personal phone referrals and pressure on Nairobi Water staff, whereas newly formalized former slum-dwellers in the Canaan KENSUP estate experience dry taps, administrative deflection between 'formal' and 'Informal Region' utility offices, inability to fund borehole deepening, and worse practical water access than in informal Kibera.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF Page 1, Abstract; PDF Pages 2–3, Introduction; PDF Pages 8–18, Sections 'Study sites', 'Concretizing water rights through infrastructural powers', 'The individualization of rights or water security beyond the state?', and 'Concluding remarks'

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the qualitative design ceiling (CASP Qualitative Checklist). Rated 2 because 12 months of multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork directly observed and documented the administrative and operational mechanisms (deflection of complaints between formal and informal utility offices, discretionary rationing and truck dispatch via personal phone networks, and unauthorized plumber connections to main lines) shaping water access.
